extracted.intended_audience: students learning to write mathematical proofs (undergraduate/introductory mathematics)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing clear, readable, and properly formatted mathematical proofs aimed at textbook/homework/exam contexts; covers audience, structure, notation, exposition, and presentation conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Every writer should have a clear idea of the intended audience for a piece of writing so the writer can give the right amount of information at the proper level of sophistication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor level of detail to audience: e.g., a solutions manual for instructors would be brief with many details omitted, while a students' solution manual should include more details. Use the audience to decide how much explanation and background to include.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with a carefully worded statement of the theorem or result
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with a simple declarative statement of the problem to be proven rather than rewriting the textbook cue (e.g., rephrase 'Prove that' as 'Theorem. ...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the theorem statement, skip a line and write 'Proof' (italics or boldface) and begin the proof on the same line. Make sure paragraphs are easily identified (skip a line or indent). Example: 'Theorem. If x is an odd integer, then x^2 is an odd integer. Proof: We assume that x is an odd integer ...'

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin the proof with a statement of your assumptions and what you will prove
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly state the assumptions you are making and immediately follow with a statement of the claim to be proven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the hypothesis and the goal clear at the outset (the text gives a fragment showing assumption of x and y odd and stating you'll prove x*y is odd). This orients the reader to the starting point and the target conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the pronoun 'we'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'we' instead of 'I' in proofs to stress collaboration with the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using 'we' encourages the reader to work through the mathematics with the author and helps engagement. Example: 'We assume that ...' rather than 'I assume that ...'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use italics for variables and proper typesetting
rubrics_metrics.description: When using a word processor, variables should be italicized; boldface for vectors; regular font for function names and mathematical words so the math looks typeset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the word processor can produce appropriate mathematical symbols and equations. Do not write 'sin x' incorrectly as 'si n x' — use proper typesetting 'sin x'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid programming-style notation for mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use '*' for multiplication or '^' for exponents; leave that notation for computer code because it is harder for humans to read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also avoid using '=' to represent division in complex fractions. Use properly formatted fractions and exponent notation instead of ASCII stand-ins. The guideline emphasizes readability: e.g., formatted fractions are easier to read than 'x^3/3x^2' style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use complete sentences and proper paragraph structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Conform to accepted rules of grammar: write proofs using complete sentences, avoid run-on sentences, include punctuation, and use a spell checker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to sentence structure and paragraphing. Good grammar is an important part of clear mathematical writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the reader informed about proof method and status of assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: State early if you will use contrapositive, contradiction, or induction. Make clear whether assertions are assumptions, previously proven results, well-known results, or from the reader's background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of early declarations: 'We will prove this result by proving the contrapositive of the statement.' 'We will prove this statement using a proof by contradiction.' 'We will use mathematical induction to prove this result.' Also explicitly indicate the provenance/status of each assertion you use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Display important equations and manipulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Center and display important equations and algebraic manipulations with blank lines before and after; do not write equations in one column with reasons in another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one side of an equation does not change across lines, avoid repeating it. Displayed equations improve readability and should be used for integral manipulations and key steps. The guideline includes a worked algebraic display example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equation numbering guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Give a number to an equation only if you will refer to it later; center and display the equation and place its number in parentheses on the same line at the right margin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the word 'equation' lowercase when referring to numbered equations (usual mathematical convention). Example: number an equation as '(1)' and later refer to it as 'equation (1)'. Don't number unnecessary equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not begin sentences with a mathematical symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid starting sentences with a symbol; instead phrase the sentence so that it begins with words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For readability, write 'An integer n is an odd integer provided that ...' rather than starting the sentence with 'n is an odd integer provided that ...' since symbol-beginning sentences can be hard to parse and may force rereading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use English words rather than cumbersome symbolic quantifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Minimize use of quantifier symbols (∀, ∃) and other compact symbols like ⇒ or ∴ in formal writing; prefer words and sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express quantification in words when it improves readability, e.g., 'For each real number x, there exists a real number y such that ...' or simply 'Every real number has an additive inverse.' Reserve symbolic shorthand for contexts where it is appropriate and clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell the reader when the proof is completed
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly indicate the end of the proof, e.g., with the sentence 'This completes the proof.' or a precise final sentence stating what has been proven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using an 'end of proof' symbol (∎ or similar) is also recommended. Making the end explicit helps the reader verify the conclusion was reached.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep it simple
rubrics_metrics.description: Use simple, declarative sentences and short paragraphs; avoid making writing more difficult than the mathematics itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each paragraph should make a single simple point. Simplicity aids comprehension even for hard mathematical arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft and revise your proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a first draft and then revise: proofs should be written so readers can follow and understand the reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be clear and concise: include necessary details without rambling. Rework and refine proofs — learning to write mathematics well takes practice. Advice: read over and refine drafts; expect difficulty and use revision to improve clarity.
